segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
My shoulder failed while I was carrying a chair.

Not fighting.

Not climbing.

Not holding a pressure door against a failing station.

Chair.

Lena's chair, technically.

She had moved across the river six months earlier and discovered that moving did not end simply because all your belongings reached the new address.

Apparently furniture continued migrating afterward.

One chair stayed at my parents' house.

My mother wanted it gone.

Lena wanted it back.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
I became transportation.

The chair was not heavy.

That mattered to my pride and nothing else.

I had a bag of groceries in my right hand, so I took the chair with my left.

The shoulder clicked.

It had clicked before rain since East Four's transfer failure. Usually one hard little movement under the joint.

Annoying.

Familiar.

This time the click became heat.

Not pain at first.

Heat.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
Then a bright line ran from the top of my shoulder to my wrist and my hand opened by itself.

The chair hit the pavement.

The groceries followed.

Three apples escaped downhill.

One rolled under a tram bench.

A boy caught it.

He looked at me.

I looked at him.

He looked at the apple.

Then ran.

I respected the decision.

My shoulder did not.

I stood very still.

People think pain makes you move.

Some pain does.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
The useful kind can make you stop so completely that breathing starts feeling like a negotiation.

I knew the difference.

First-life Greg had broken shoulders before.

Other people's.

Once mine.

Different shoulder.

Different mechanism.

Different body.

Memory still offered instructions immediately.

Rotate inward.

Set the scapula.

Reinforce around the joint.

Pull through the back instead of the arm.

Old-body advice.

Bad advice.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
I tried the smallest part of it anyway.

White light went through my teeth.

"Fuck."

A woman passing with a basket stopped.

"You all right?"

"Yes."

My left arm hung six inches away from my side.

The chair lay in the road.

Two apples were gone.

She looked at all of that.

"No."

"Fair."

She helped me get the chair against a wall.

I used my right hand.

That was when I discovered I could walk perfectly well while furious.

Useful information.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
I went home instead of Lena's.

That was my first correct decision.

I nearly ruined it by deciding home meant I could fix the shoulder myself.

Nessa was not there.

Three days each week she covered district transfer coordination now. Not a promotion, according to the station, because institutions prefer words that do not imply money.

It meant six crews could all want the same pressure window and Nessa got paid to tell five of them no.

She was good at it.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
I put the groceries on the table.

One apple remained.

Bad survival rate.

Then I found the broom.

Do not ask.

I had tried a broom handle after the original transfer injury years before.

It had not worked then either.

This was available evidence.

I ignored it.

I wedged the handle under my left arm and tried to lift the shoulder from below.

The joint moved half an inch.

Pain reached the back of my skull.

I sat down very quickly.

The broom fell.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
Then the door opened.

Of course.

Nessa came in carrying two work slates and stopped.

She looked at me.

The broom.

My arm.

The groceries.

One apple.

Her face went through several emotions and chose murder.

"No."

"I haven't said anything."

"You are doing the broom."

"It almost worked."

"You said that last time."

"It moved."

"You screamed."

"Quietly."

She put the slates down.

"Can you move your fingers?"

"Yes."

"Hand numb?"

"No."

"Neck?"

"Fine."

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
"Chest?"

"Fine."

"Shoulder?"

"Bad."

"That one I had."

She crouched in front of me.

"Did it come out?"

"No."

"You sure?"

"Yes."

"Based on?"

"I know what a dislocation feels like."

Nessa narrowed her eyes.

"Which body?"

Asshole.

"This one has done it too."

"Good. Current evidence."

I hated that our rules had become conversational weapons.

She touched the top of the shoulder.

I flinched before she pressed.

"That's not good."

"I know."

"Healer."

"No."

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
"Greg."

"It will settle."

"Current evidence?"

I looked at her.

She waited.

Nothing.

"It usually settles."

"Historical evidence."

"Still evidence."

"From the shoulder that currently cannot carry an apple?"

"That child stole one."

"What?"

"Nothing."

She stood.

"We're going."

"No."

Then I tried to stand.

My shoulder shifted.

I sat again.

Nessa nodded.

"Compelling."

The healer said tendon inflammation, scar adhesion, and probable joint irritation.
